title: Experimental Biology I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L introductory biology practical curriculum: microscope use and care, laboratory safety, specimen/slide preparation and staining, qualitative food (biochemical) tests, and basic osmosis/diffusion demonstrations.

questions.question: In a compound light microscope, the total magnification of a specimen is calculated as:
options: Eyepiece lens magnification multiplied by objective lens magnification
Eyepiece lens magnification added to objective lens magnification
Objective lens magnification divided by eyepiece lens magnification
Stage micrometer reading multiplied by focal length
questions.correct_answer: Eyepiece lens magnification multiplied by objective lens magnification
questions.explanation: Total magnification equals the magnifying power of the eyepiece (ocular) lens multiplied by that of the objective lens in use.

questions.question: When beginning to view any new slide under a compound microscope, the correct practice is to:
options: Start with the lowest power (scanning) objective and increase magnification progressively
Start with the oil immersion objective for the clearest first view
Start with the highest power objective to save time
Remove the eyepiece before focusing
questions.correct_answer: Start with the lowest power (scanning) objective and increase magnification progressively
questions.explanation: Starting at low power gives a wider field of view to locate the specimen safely before switching to higher magnifications for detail.

questions.question: The iris diaphragm of a compound microscope primarily functions to:
options: Regulate the amount of light passing through the specimen
Hold the slide firmly in place on the stage
Magnify the image of the specimen
Focus the image sharply
questions.correct_answer: Regulate the amount of light passing through the specimen
questions.explanation: The iris diaphragm, located beneath the stage, can be opened or closed to control the intensity of light illuminating the specimen.

questions.question: The coarse and fine adjustment knobs on a compound microscope are used to:
options: Bring the specimen into sharp focus by raising or lowering the stage or body tube
Control the amount of light reaching the specimen
Change the objective lens in use
Clean the lenses
questions.correct_answer: Bring the specimen into sharp focus by raising or lowering the stage or body tube
questions.explanation: The coarse adjustment gives large focusing movements, while the fine adjustment allows small, precise movements to sharpen the image.

questions.question: Resolution, as distinct from magnification, refers to a microscope's ability to:
options: Distinguish two closely spaced points as separate objects
Enlarge the apparent size of a specimen
Focus on thick specimens without cutting sections
Increase the brightness of the image
questions.correct_answer: Distinguish two closely spaced points as separate objects
questions.explanation: Resolution (resolving power) is the capacity to show fine detail by distinguishing between two very close points, which is not the same as simply enlarging the image (magnification).

questions.question: When preparing a temporary wet mount of a specimen, the coverslip should be lowered onto the drop of water/stain at an angle mainly to:
options: Reduce the trapping of air bubbles under the coverslip
Increase the magnification of the image
Sterilize the specimen
Prevent the stain from working
questions.correct_answer: Reduce the trapping of air bubbles under the coverslip
questions.explanation: Lowering a coverslip at an angle, edge first, allows air to escape rather than becoming trapped as bubbles that would obscure the specimen.

questions.question: The oil immersion objective lens is used with a drop of immersion oil mainly to:
options: Improve resolution by reducing the refraction (bending) of light between the slide and lens
Clean the objective lens
Increase the amount of light reaching the eyepiece only
Prevent the slide from drying out
questions.correct_answer: Improve resolution by reducing the refraction (bending) of light between the slide and lens
questions.explanation: Immersion oil has a refractive index close to that of glass, minimising light scattering and allowing the oil immersion objective to achieve its very high resolution.

questions.question: A student focuses a specimen under the low power objective (x10) with an eyepiece of x10, then switches to the high power objective (x40). The new total magnification is:
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification x objective magnification = 10 x 40 = 400.

questions.question: Before starting any practical work in the biology laboratory, a student should FIRST:
options: Put on appropriate protective wear (e.g. lab coat) and note the location of safety equipment
Begin heating any chemicals to be used
Taste any unlabeled solution to identify it
Leave bags and personal belongings on the bench beside the apparatus
questions.correct_answer: Put on appropriate protective wear (e.g. lab coat) and note the location of safety equipment
questions.explanation: Basic laboratory safety requires wearing protective clothing and being aware of safety equipment (fire extinguisher, first aid kit) before handling any specimens or reagents.

questions.question: Broken glassware in the biology laboratory should be:
options: Swept up carefully (never picked up by hand) and disposed of in a designated sharps/glass container
Left on the floor until the end of the day
Picked up immediately with bare hands
Disposed of in the general classroom waste bin
questions.correct_answer: Swept up carefully (never picked up by hand) and disposed of in a designated sharps/glass container
questions.explanation: Broken glass poses a cutting hazard and must be handled with a brush/dustpan and disposed of in a container specifically meant for sharps to prevent injury.

questions.question: Before using any chemical reagent from a stock bottle in a practical, a student should always:
options: Read the label carefully to confirm the reagent and its concentration
Smell it directly by placing the nose over the open bottle
Mix it immediately with any other reagent on the bench
Assume its identity based on the bottle's shape
questions.correct_answer: Read the label carefully to confirm the reagent and its concentration
questions.explanation: Confirming the reagent's identity and concentration from its label prevents dangerous mix-ups and ensures the correct experimental procedure.

questions.question: Staining is commonly used in preparing biological specimens for microscopy mainly to:
options: Increase the contrast of cell structures that would otherwise be nearly transparent and hard to see
Kill any living cells before observation
Increase the size of the specimen
Preserve the specimen permanently without a coverslip
questions.correct_answer: Increase the contrast of cell structures that would otherwise be nearly transparent and hard to see
questions.explanation: Most cells and their internal structures are colourless and transparent; stains bind differentially to structures like the nucleus, making them visible against the background.

questions.question: In a practical examining onion epidermal cells, iodine solution is commonly applied mainly to stain the:
options: Nucleus, making it more visible
Cell wall only
Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
questions.correct_answer: Nucleus, making it more visible
questions.explanation: Iodine solution stains the nucleus of onion epidermal cells a yellowish-brown colour, helping students locate it clearly under the microscope.

questions.question: Methylene blue is a stain commonly used in practicals to make visible the nuclei of:
options: Human cheek epithelial cells
Starch grains in potato
Bacterial spores specifically
Plant chloroplasts
questions.correct_answer: Human cheek epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Methylene blue is routinely used to stain a smear of human cheek cells, colouring the nucleus and making cell outlines easier to observe under the microscope.

questions.question: In Benedict's test for reducing sugars, a positive result is indicated by the formation of a:
options: Brick-red (orange-red) precipitate after heating
Deep blue-black colour at room temperature
Violet/purple ring at the interface of two liquids
White, milky emulsion layer
questions.correct_answer: Brick-red (orange-red) precipitate after heating
questions.explanation: Reducing sugars reduce the blue copper(II) sulfate in Benedict's reagent to insoluble red copper(I) oxide on heating, producing a brick-red precipitate.

questions.question: The presence of starch in a food sample is confirmed by adding iodine solution, which produces a:
options: Blue-black colour
Brick-red precipitate
Violet/purple colour
White emulsion
questions.correct_answer: Blue-black colour
questions.explanation: Iodine forms a characteristic blue-black complex with starch, a classic and highly specific test for its presence.

questions.question: The Biuret test is used to test for the presence of proteins in a sample; a positive result is shown by a colour change to:
options: Violet/purple
Brick-red
Blue-black
Yellow
questions.correct_answer: Violet/purple
questions.explanation: In the Biuret test, copper(II) ions in an alkaline solution form a violet/purple complex with peptide bonds, indicating the presence of protein.

questions.question: The emulsion (ethanol) test is used to test a food sample for the presence of:
options: Lipids (fats/oils)
Reducing sugars
Starch
Proteins
questions.correct_answer: Lipids (fats/oils)
questions.explanation: When a fat-containing sample is dissolved in ethanol and then added to water, lipids form a visible cloudy white emulsion, indicating their presence.

questions.question: A food sample gives a negative Benedict's test directly, but tests positive for reducing sugar after the sample is first boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid and then neutralised. This indicates the original sample contains a:
options: Non-reducing sugar (e.g. sucrose), which is hydrolysed by the acid into reducing sugars
Protein only
Lipid only
Reducing sugar that was destroyed by boiling
questions.correct_answer: Non-reducing sugar (e.g. sucrose), which is hydrolysed by the acid into reducing sugars
questions.explanation: Non-reducing sugars like sucrose do not react with Benedict's reagent directly, but acid hydrolysis breaks them into reducing monosaccharides that then give a positive test.

questions.question: Which reagent is used in the standard laboratory test to detect reducing sugars in a food sample?
options: Benedict's solution
Biuret reagent
Iodine solution
Ethanol
questions.correct_answer: Benedict's solution
questions.explanation: Benedict's solution, containing copper(II) sulfate, is the standard reagent used and heated with a sample to test for reducing sugars.

questions.question: In an osmosis experiment demonstrating a semi-permeable membrane, Visking (dialysis) tubing is commonly used because it:
options: Allows small molecules like water to pass through but retains larger molecules such as starch
Is completely impermeable to all substances
Allows all molecules, regardless of size, to pass through freely
Actively pumps water from one side to the other
questions.correct_answer: Allows small molecules like water to pass through but retains larger molecules such as starch
questions.explanation: Visking tubing has tiny pores that mimic a cell's selectively/semi-permeable membrane, letting small molecules like water diffuse through while excluding larger molecules.

questions.question: In the classic potato osmometer/cylinder experiment, potato tissue placed in a concentrated (hypertonic) sugar or salt solution will:
options: Lose mass and become flaccid as water leaves the cells by osmosis
Gain mass and become turgid as water enters the cells
Show no change in mass at all
Immediately burst due to excess water uptake
questions.correct_answer: Lose mass and become flaccid as water leaves the cells by osmosis
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic external solution, water moves out of the potato cells by osmosis (from higher to lower water potential), causing the tissue to lose mass and become flaccid.

questions.question: When plant cells are placed in a hypotonic (dilute) solution, water enters by osmosis and the cells typically become:
options: Turgid, as the cell membrane presses against the rigid cell wall
Plasmolysed, as the cell membrane pulls away from the wall
Lysed (burst), just as an animal cell would
Completely unchanged
questions.correct_answer: Turgid, as the cell membrane presses against the rigid cell wall
questions.explanation: Because plant cells have a rigid cell wall, water entering by osmosis increases internal pressure until the wall resists further expansion, producing turgidity rather than bursting.

questions.question: Unlike a plant cell, an animal cell (e.g. a red blood cell) placed in a very hypotonic (distilled water) solution will typically:
options: Swell and eventually burst (lyse), since it lacks a rigid cell wall
Become turgid but never burst
Shrink and crenate
Remain completely unaffected
questions.correct_answer: Swell and eventually burst (lyse), since it lacks a rigid cell wall
questions.explanation: Without a supporting cell wall, continued water entry into an animal cell in a hypotonic solution causes the plasma membrane to stretch until it ruptures (lysis).

questions.question: Which apparatus would be most appropriate for accurately measuring a small, precise volume of liquid reagent (e.g. 2 cm3) in a practical?
options: A graduated pipette
A beaker
A test tube
A microscope slide
questions.correct_answer: A graduated pipette
questions.explanation: A graduated (or volumetric) pipette is designed for measuring and transferring small, precise volumes of liquid, unlike a beaker or test tube which give only rough estimates.

questions.question: A hand lens (magnifying glass) is most appropriately used in a biology practical to:
options: Examine the external features of a specimen at low magnification in the field or on the bench
View the internal ultrastructure of a single cell
Replace the compound microscope for all observations
Measure the exact mass of a specimen
questions.correct_answer: Examine the external features of a specimen at low magnification in the field or on the bench
questions.explanation: A hand lens provides modest magnification useful for quickly examining external morphology, without the setup needed for a compound microscope.

questions.question: A dichotomous key used in classification practicals works by:
options: Presenting a series of paired statements/questions, each choice leading to the next step until the specimen is identified
Listing every organism's full scientific description in alphabetical order
Grouping organisms solely by their habitat
Using only DNA sequence data to identify a specimen
questions.correct_answer: Presenting a series of paired statements/questions, each choice leading to the next step until the specimen is identified
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key guides identification through a sequence of either/or choices about observable characteristics, narrowing down to a single identification.

questions.question: A vernier caliper is used in a biology practical mainly to:
options: Take precise linear measurements (e.g. length, diameter) of a specimen, more accurately than an ordinary ruler
Measure the pH of a solution
Determine the mass of a specimen
Count the number of cells in a tissue sample
questions.correct_answer: Take precise linear measurements (e.g. length, diameter) of a specimen, more accurately than an ordinary ruler
questions.explanation: A vernier caliper allows measurement of length or diameter to a finer precision (often 0.1 mm or better) than a standard ruler.

questions.question: A student records the observation, drawing, and label of a specimen in a practical notebook. Biological drawings in a practical report should be made using:
options: Clear, single continuous lines in pencil, with labels connected by straight, non-crossing lines
Shading and colouring to make the drawing artistic
Sketchy, overlapping lines to show texture
No labels, since the drawing should be self-explanatory
questions.correct_answer: Clear, single continuous lines in pencil, with labels connected by straight, non-crossing lines
questions.explanation: Standard biological drawing convention uses clean pencil outlines without shading, with straight label lines that do not cross, for scientific clarity and accuracy.
